The Spigot Algorithm for Pi

AlgorithmsPlace ValueInfinite Series
Game: Watch the digits of pi come out one at a time, like water from a tap.
How to play: Say how many digits you want and press Compute. Stop and Continue whenever you like.

Look for the math

A spigot algorithm lets digits drip out one at a time and never looks at them again. Stanley Rabinowitz found one for pi in 1991, and he and Stan Wagon studied it in 1995.

Pi in a strange number system

A decimal number is a nest of tenths: π = 3 + 1/10 (1 + 1/10 (4 + 1/10 (1 + …))), the form Horner's method uses. A classical series for pi can be nested the same way:

π = 2 + 1/3 (2 + 2/5 (2 + 3/7 (2 + 4/9 (2 + …))))

Read as a mixed-radix number with place values 1/3, 2/5, 3/7, …, pi is simply 2.2222…. The algorithm converts it to base 10.

Converting, one digit at a time

To get the next decimal digit, multiply every place by 10, then tidy up from the right. Place i may only hold less than 2i + 1; what overflows is carried left, worth (i−1)/(2i−1) as much. The leftmost place then holds the next digit, plus a remainder that stays. An array of [10n/3] + 1 places, every one starting at 2, is enough for n digits.

Holding back the nines

Sometimes the next digit comes out as 10, so 1 must be added to the digit before it, and if that was a 9 it becomes 0 and the 1 goes further left. So the algorithm holds a digit back while it is followed by 9s and prints them only when a digit other than 9 or 10 shows that no carry can reach them. Both cases happen in the first 800 digits, and the logic test checked every run of up to 400 digits, and runs of 1000 and 3000, against pi worked out another way (Machin's formula). With only [10n/3] places, Rabinowitz and Wagon's first count, the runs of 1 and 32 digits come out wrong. That is Arndt and Haenel's reason for the extra place.

Ask for 770 digits and look near the end for six 9s in a row, the Feynman point. Watch how they wait before they are printed.
